guidance.label: Exterior Walls / Siding
guidance.summary: Flood damage to wood exterior walls and siding is usually not serious as long as the wood is allowed to dry out afterward; the real danger comes from moisture that gets trapped and cannot evaporate, such as in wall cavities, behind insulation, or under impermeable paint finishes.

do.text: Let flood-saturated wood siding and framing dry out in place rather than assuming it needs replacement, since a one-time flood event usually does little lasting harm if the wood can dry.

citations.quote: Damage from a one-time event, such as a flood, is usually negligible if the wood is allowed to air dry.

do.text: Remove insulation from around wall sill areas so trapped water can evaporate and the wood framing can dry.

citations.quote: Remove insulation at sill and allow wood to dry.

do.text: Clear out any mud or silt left inside wall cavities, whether or not the insulation itself is removed.

citations.quote: Any mud or silt that remains in the cavity should be removed regardless of the insulation’s condition.

do.text: Plan to remove insulation that sat in floodwater: with few exceptions, it should come out. Closed-cell styrene or urethane board, which doesn't absorb water, can sometimes stay, but inspect it and remove it until everything dries if it holds moisture against wood, masonry, or steel fasteners.

citations.quote: With few exceptions, any insulation that has been immersed in water should be removed
Some types of insulation may be left in place after water contact, such as closed-cell styrene and urethane board insulations that do not absorb water.
whether they hold moisture against wood or masonry materials or steel fasteners. If so, the insulation should be removed until all materials are dry.

do.text: Watch for moisture getting trapped inside walls behind finishes or in cavities, since that trapped dampness, not the one-time flooding itself, is what causes lasting wood damage.

citations.quote: Problems occur when moisture is trapped in the wood and cannot escape.

dont.text: Don't leave saturated insulation sitting inside wall cavities, since it holds water that can keep wood, masonry, and steel destructively damp.

citations.quote: Saturated insulation holds water which, if left in place, can perpetuate high moisture conditions destructive to wood, masonry, and steel.

dont.text: Don't seal damp wall assemblies back up behind impermeable finishes like oil-based gloss paint, or leave them enclosed in cavities and under floors, without letting them dry first.

citations.quote: This can happen in wall cavities, in sill plates under floors, behind panelling and under impermeable finishes such as oil-based gloss paint.

dont.text: Don't leave fiberglass batt insulation in place if it is blocking airflow through the wall cavity and slowing the drying-out process.

citations.quote: if they impede the flow of air in a wall cavity, and thus the drying-out process, it may be necessary to remove them.

dont.text: Don't let wood moisture levels stay elevated indefinitely; moisture content above roughly 28 percent creates conditions where dry rot spores could germinate.

citations.quote: If the moisture content exceeds 28 per cent then dry rot spores could germinate.

guidance.label: Windows and Doors
guidance.summary: Flood-damaged historic windows and doors can often be saved rather than replaced if they are handled carefully during drying and cleanup. Original wood trim and panel doors tend to survive flooding better than expected and typically return to their original form once fully dried.

do.text: Retain original wood trim around baseboards, ceilings, doors, and windows, since it typically survives a flood and should return to its original form once dried.

citations.quote: Wood trim around baseboards, ceilings, doors, and windows is likely to survive a flood

citations.source_file: treatment of flood damaged hist buildings.pdf
citations.quote: After drying, it should return to its original form and should be retained.

do.text: Recognize that wooden doors in older and historic buildings are typically panel doors that contribute to the building's character, and weigh this when deciding on repair versus replacement.

citations.quote: Wooden doors in older and historic buildings are likely to be panel doors that add to the character of the building.

do.text: If a door cannot be saved and must be replaced, replicate the original panel door design rather than installing a generic replacement.

citations.source_file: treatment of flood damaged hist buildings.pdf
citations.quote: If you need to replace any doors, consider replicating original panel doors.

do.text: Where a large historic window opening extends below the established flood risk level, use engineered structural reinforcing at the opening rather than removing or eliminating it.

citations.quote: the structural reinforcing required at large window openings that extend below the established flood risk level.

do.text: Consider removable exterior storm windows over historic sash, and for stained glass use only ventilated storm units, so the cavity between the storm and the historic window can still be periodically vented.

citations.quote: removable exterior storm windows, but allow operation of windows for periodic ventilation of cavity between exterior storm and historic sash.
For stained glass windows using protective glazing, use only ventilated storms to avoid condensation as well as heat build-up.

dont.text: Don't attempt to repair or plane flood-affected doors until they are completely dry.

citations.quote: Be sure that the doors are completely dry before attempting to repair or plane them.

dont.text: Don't count on hollow-core doors surviving a flood; their internal spacers are usually cardboard, which dissolves in water, so plan on replacement.

citations.source_file: treatment of flood damaged hist buildings.pdf
citations.quote: Hollow core doors will likely need to be replaced because their internal spacers are usually made of cardboard which dissolves in water.

dont.text: Don't apply sealants to wood while drying and treating for mold after a flood.

citations.quote: Other fungicides may also help inhibit mold regrowth during drying. Do not apply sealants to wood.

dont.text: Don't default to permanently or temporarily blocking large historic window openings that extend below the flood risk level; reinforced glazing alternatives have been used instead of blocking.

citations.quote: Rather than blocking these windows, either permanently or temporarily, the owner elected to use aquarium glass in the lower sash.

guidance.label: Chimney
guidance.summary: Historic masonry chimneys are especially vulnerable after a flood because their lime mortar can be eroded or washed out by floodwater, and any embedded metal is prone to rusting once wet. Once the water recedes and materials dry, inspect the mortar joints, embedded metal, and overall condition before deciding what to repair.

do.text: After floodwater recedes and materials dry, check the mortar joints near lintels for cracking or loss, and repoint promptly so water can't get in and cause further rusting of embedded metal.

citations.source_file: treatment of flood damaged hist buildings.pdf
citations.quote: check the mortar joints near the lintels to see that the mortar has not cracked or fallen out

citations.source_file: treatment of flood damaged hist buildings.pdf
citations.quote: If it has, repoint the area immediately to make sure that water cannot enter to create further rusting.

do.text: Before repointing over embedded metal, scrape off any loose rust scale, and periodically inspect embedded iron-based metal in the masonry, repairing any surrounding cracks that develop.

citations.source_file: treatment of flood damaged hist buildings.pdf
citations.quote: Before repointing, scrape the metal to remove any loose rust scale.

citations.source_file: treatment of flood damaged hist buildings.pdf
citations.quote: If other iron-based metals are imbedded in masonry or concrete, inspect them periodically and repair cracks in the surrounding materials if they occur.

do.text: Remove deteriorated lime mortar by hand raking the joints, a careful approach that avoids damaging the surrounding historic masonry.

citations.quote: Removing deteriorated lime mortar carefully by hand raking the joints to avoid damaging

do.text: As part of routine maintenance, remove efflorescence (salt deposits) from the chimney's masonry using non-metallic bristle brushes.

citations.quote: remove efflorescence from masonry with non-metallic bristle brushes

dont.text: Don't remove sound, non-deteriorated mortar from the chimney or repoint the whole structure just to make it look uniform.

citations.quote: Removing non-deteriorated mortar from sound features by repointing the mortar joints

dont.text: Don't repoint flood-damaged historic chimney masonry with impermeable, heavily cement-based mortar, since it holds moisture in the masonry longer and can cause salts to crystallize within the historic material.

citations.quote: Impermeable, heavily cement-based mortar will exacerbate deterioration during a flood because it holds the moisture in the masonry for longer and causes salts to crystallise within the historic materials.

dont.text: Don't leave flood-soaked chimney masonry wet going into freezing conditions, since spalling of soft brick or stone typically occurs when temperatures drop below freezing while moisture is still trapped in the walls.

citations.quote: The spalling of soft brick or stonework usually occurs on building exteriors when the temperature drops below freezing while moisture is still trapped within walls.

guidance.label: Insulation
guidance.summary: Insulation that gets wet during a flood tends to stay wet long after visible surfaces look dry, which can hide mold and decay growth inside historic wall cavities. Removing saturated fibrous insulation and any trapped mud or silt, then opening the cavity to ventilate, helps walls dry out. Not every material needs to go.

do.text: Remove all wet fibrous insulation, even if the wallboard or wall covering appears to be dry.

citations.quote: Remove all wet fibrous insulation—even if wallboard appears to be dry.

do.text: Remove moldy porous materials and bag them to reduce the spread of mold spores.

citations.quote: Porous moldy or sewage-contaminated materials should be removed, put in plastic bags if possible, and thrown away.

do.text: Remove any mud or silt left in the wall cavity, regardless of the insulation's condition.

citations.quote: Any mud or silt that remains in the cavity should be removed regardless of the insulation’s condition.

do.text: Cut holes in plaster or wallboard to remove wall insulation, and leave the holes open to ventilate the cavity.

citations.quote: Cut holes in plaster or wallboard and remove wall insulation. Leave holes open to ventilate wall cavities.

do.text: Remove fiberglass batts along with other wet fibrous insulation. Glass fibers don't absorb water themselves, but batts that block airflow in the wall cavity slow the drying-out process.

citations.quote: Remove all wet fibrous insulation—even if wallboard appears to be dry.
Glass fibers, in themselves, are not water absorbent, but if they impede the flow of air in a wall cavity, and thus the drying-out process, it may be necessary to remove them.

do.text: Keep dry, undamaged plaster, wood paneling, or non-paper-faced gypsum board walls with no insulation behind them by cleaning and sanitizing rather than removing them.

citations.quote: Plaster, wood paneling, and non-paper faced gypsum board walls that are dry, in good condition, and have no insulation in the wall can be cleaned and sanitized to salvage them.

dont.text: Don't assume that dry-looking wallboard means the insulation behind it is dry, since wet insulation stays wet far too long and can breed hidden mold and decay fungi inside the walls.

citations.quote: Wet insulation will stay wet far too long, leading to the growth of hidden unhealthy mold and decay fungi inside the walls.

dont.text: Don't leave wet insulation packed against wood, masonry, or steel fasteners, since it holds moisture, keeps the inside of the wall wet, creates conditions for rotting, and rusts steel nails.

citations.quote: Wet insulation holds moisture keeping inside of the wall wet and creating conditions for rotting.
Wet insulation packed between joists of sill plate keeps wood saturated and rusts steel nails.

dont.text: Don't leave heavily mold-affected porous materials in place hoping to salvage them; it's best to remove them, especially with heavy or long-term mold growth.

citations.quote: It’s best to remove all moldly porous materials, especially if there is heavy or long-term mold growth

guidance.label: Interior Finishes
guidance.summary: Flood-damaged historic interior finishes such as plaster, wallpaper, and flooring can often be saved, but each material needs to dry fully before you decide whether to repair, retain, or replace it. When a finish truly cannot be saved, keep documented samples so the historic material is preserved for the record.

do.text: Recognize that older, historic wallpaper can often be saved after a flood, even though deciding whether to retain or remove it is a difficult call.

citations.quote: In many cases, older and historic wallpaper may be saved after a flood, but the decision to retain or remove it is a difficult one.

do.text: Before removing damaged wallpaper, take samples from several different spots, including the ceiling, so you have a documented record of the pattern and material.

citations.quote: take samples from several different locations including the ceiling

do.text: Store any wallpaper samples you remove in a dry part of the house until they can be properly preserved.

citations.quote: store temporarily in a dry part of the house until the paper can be permanently preserved

do.text: Inspect plaster walls and ceilings for broken plaster keys, since moisture-swollen wood lath is a known cause of this kind of failure.

citations.quote: Moisture causes wood lath to expand and deform, causing plaster keys to break off.

do.text: Let plaster dry out fully and then inspect it before deciding whether it needs to be replaced.

citations.source_file: treatment of flood damaged hist buildings.pdf
citations.quote: the best way to determine whether plaster must be replaced is to let it dry and then inspect it

do.text: For historically significant sheet flooring like linoleum, let it dry and check that it is level and still adhered before deciding to leave it in place.

citations.quote: Once dry, if the floor is level and the flooring adheres, you may leave it in place.

dont.text: Don't stand directly beneath an area of plaster you are prodding to drain, since the plaster may loosen and fall.

citations.source_file: treatment of flood damaged hist buildings.pdf
citations.quote: Do not stand directly under the area being prodded in case the plaster loosens and falls.

dont.text: Don't judge whether plaster is sound just by looking at its surface condition.

citations.source_file: treatment of flood damaged hist buildings.pdf
citations.quote: The surface condition of plaster may not tell you whether it is sound.

dont.text: Don't throw away historic flooring that can't be re-laid without first saving samples of it.

citations.quote: If it is impossible to re-lay the floor, make sure to save samples of the historic flooring.

guidance.label: Structural / Foundation
guidance.summary: Flood damage to foundations is one of the most dangerous situations a homeowner can face. Water exerts tremendous hydrostatic pressure on foundation walls, and pumping a flooded basement too soon can cause walls to collapse inward. Inspect masonry mortar joints for erosion, replace eroded soil around the foundation, and always consult a structural engineer before making repairs.

do.text: Be aware that pumping water from a flooded basement can be dangerous — the water inside may be balancing the hydrostatic pressure of groundwater outside, and removing it too quickly can cause foundation walls to collapse.

citations.quote: pumping water from your basement can be dangerous. This water may be providing the necessary pressure to balance the hydrostatic pressure of the groundwater

do.text: Leave water in a flooded basement until the groundwater table drops and the water recedes on its own, rather than pumping it out while exterior groundwater levels are still high.

citations.quote: It is advisable to leave the water in place until the groundwater table sinks and the water recedes by itself

do.text: Inspect the mortar of stone masonry foundation walls to check whether it has been washed out of the joints, which can make the wall unstable.

citations.quote: Inspect the mortar of stone masonry foundation walls to ensure that it has not leeched from the joints and made the wall unstable

do.text: Replace eroded soil around foundation walls and restore positive drainage away from the building to prevent ongoing water damage.

citations.quote: Eroded soil at foundation wall leads to continuing water damage
Fill with soil to provide positive drainage away from building

do.text: When repointing sandstone or soft stone foundations, use a lime-rich mortar (at least two parts hydrated lime to one part white Portland cement and nine parts sand — ASTM Type O) so the mortar is softer than the surrounding stone.

citations.quote: new mortar should contain at least two parts hydrated lime to each part of white Portland cement and nine parts sand

do.text: Inspect brick masonry and concrete block foundation walls for missing mortar and repair them, especially if there is reason to suspect structural problems from the flooding.

citations.quote: they should be inspected for missing mortar and repaired in the same manner as aboveground walls, unless there is reason to suspect a more serious structural problem created by the flooding

do.text: If FEMA helps with flood repairs, expect limited help for a basement (a floor below ground level on all sides). FEMA home repair in basements is limited to damage that affects the home's safety, sanitation, and functionality, such as the foundation and critical utilities like the furnace or water heater. Wet or moldy drywall, carpet, or cabinets in non-essential basement areas are covered for removal only.

citations.quote: FEMA defines a basement as an area of the home with its floor below grade (below ground level) on all sides.
Home Repair Assistance for flood-damaged real property in basements is limited to damaged items that result in living conditions affecting the safety, sanitation, and functionality of the home.
Damage to the structural components (e.g., foundation) of the home
Damage to critical utilities that support the overall function of the home (e.g., furnace, water heater)
Damage presenting a hazard (e.g., wet or moldy drywall, carpet, or cabinets) in non-essential living areas (for removal only)

dont.text: Do not pump a flooded basement if the groundwater outside is still high — the foundation walls could be pushed inward and collapse from unbalanced hydrostatic pressure.

citations.quote: If the groundwater level is higher than your basement floor and you pump the water from your basement, the foundation walls could be pushed inward and collapse

dont.text: Do not underestimate the pressure that water exerts on below-grade walls and floor slabs — even standing water in a basement may be preventing structural failure.

citations.quote: Water can exert tremendous pressure on foundation walls and floor slabs

guidance.call_a_pro: Consult a licensed structural engineer before making any foundation or structural repairs. If walls are cracked, settling, or showing signs of movement, get a professional assessment before re-occupying the building.

guidance.label: Electrical / Mechanical / HVAC
guidance.summary: Flood-damaged electrical, mechanical, and HVAC systems pose immediate life-safety risks. All power must be confirmed off before entering, and any submerged wiring must be professionally inspected before the power is restored. When planning repairs, relocate utilities above the established flood risk level to protect them in future events.

do.text: Make sure all electricity is turned off before entering a flood-damaged building, and have any submerged electrical wiring inspected by a licensed electrician before restoring power.

citations.quote: Make sure that all of your electricity is turned off. If any electrical wiring was submerged, have it inspected before turning the power back on

do.text: Stay away from downed power lines and electrical wires in and around the flood area.

citations.quote: Stay away from power lines and electrical wires

do.text: If using generators or charcoal grills during cleanup, make sure they are properly vented to prevent carbon monoxide poisoning.

citations.quote: Carbon monoxide exhaust kills. If you use electrical generators or charcoal grills, make sure that they are properly vented

do.text: Elevate or relocate utilities and mechanical systems above the established flood risk level, placing them in utilitarian or insignificant spaces in the building that are unlikely to flood.

citations.quote: Any part of these systems that is in flood-vulnerable locations should be elevated or relocated above the established flood risk level
Utilities and mechanical systems should be relocated to utilitarian or insignificant spaces in historic buildings that are unlikely to flood

do.text: Consider installing an electrical disconnect well above the flood risk level, separate from the main utility panel, so power to flood-prone areas can be cut quickly.

citations.quote: Installing an electrical disconnect well above the established flood risk level in an easy to access location. This should be separate from the utility panel

do.text: When planning any project involving mechanical, electrical, plumbing, or fire suppression systems, consider the service life of the various system components so you can plan upgrades strategically.

citations.quote: When planning a project involving mechanical, electrical, plumbing, or fire suppression systems, it is helpful to be aware of the service life of the various features of the systems involved

dont.text: Do not damage or destroy historic interior or exterior features excessively when accessing wall cavities for re-wiring — plan electrical work to minimize impact on historic character.

citations.quote: Damaging or destroying historic interior or exterior features, finishes, or materials to an excessive degree in order to access wall cavities for re-wiring

guidance.call_a_pro: All submerged electrical, mechanical, and HVAC systems must be fully inspected and recertified by licensed professionals before use. This is a life-safety issue — do not attempt electrical repairs yourself.

guidance.label: Mold / Contamination
guidance.summary: Mold can begin to grow on materials that stay wet longer than two or three days after a flood. The longer it grows, the greater the health hazard and the harder it is to control. Prompt cleanup, proper protective equipment, and careful isolation of affected areas are essential. For large infestations, hire a licensed mold remediation contractor.

do.text: Begin cleanup as soon as it is safe to return — mold grows rapidly on materials that stay wet, and the longer it grows, the greater the health hazard and the harder it is to control.

citations.quote: grow on materials that stay wet longer than two or three days. The longer it grows, the greater the health hazard and the harder it is to control

do.text: Wear gloves, goggles, and a respirator rated N-95 or higher when working in mold-affected areas, since people are mainly exposed by breathing spores and skin contact.

citations.quote: People are mainly exposed to mold by breathing spores and skin contact. Wear gloves, goggles, and a respirator rated N-95 or higher

do.text: Seal off moldy areas from the rest of the house before disturbing mold colonies, and ventilate to outdoors — do not run the central air system during cleanup.

citations.quote: seal off the moldy areas from the rest of the house. Open windows, and don't run the central air system

do.text: Tape plastic over air grilles and drape plastic in stairwells to isolate clean areas. If power is on, put a fan in a window to exhaust mold-filled air to the outdoors.

citations.quote: Tape plastic over air grilles, and drape plastic in the stairwell if the second story is dry and clean. If power is on, put a fan in a window to blow out and exhaust mold-filled air to the outdoors

do.text: Remove all porous, moldy, or sewage-contaminated materials — bag them in plastic before removing to reduce the release and spread of spores.

citations.quote: Porous moldy or sewage-contaminated materials should be removed, put in plastic bags if possible, and thrown away

do.text: Remove all flooded carpeting, upholstery, fabrics, and mattresses right away — discard them or have them professionally cleaned and dried quickly outside the home.

citations.quote: Remove all flooded carpeting, upholstery, fabrics, and mattresses right away

do.text: Remove all wet fibrous insulation from walls, even if the wallboard appears dry — wet insulation stays wet far too long and leads to hidden mold and decay fungi.

citations.quote: Remove all wet fibrous insulation—even if wallboard appears to be dry. Wet insulation will stay wet far too long, leading to the growth of hidden unhealthy mold and decay fungi inside the walls

do.text: Clean mold from non-porous surfaces (hard plastic, concrete, glass, metal, solid wood) — cleaning should remove the mold, not just kill it, because dead spores can still cause health problems.

citations.quote: Surface mold can be effectively cleaned from non-porous materials such as hard plastic, concrete, glass, and metal. Solid wood can also be cleaned
Cleaning should remove, not just kill, the mold, because dead spores can still cause health problems

do.text: Take photographs for insurance purposes before cleaning up — do not wait for the claims adjuster before removing wet and moldy materials.

citations.quote: Take photographs for insurance purposes before cleaning up. Do not wait for the claims adjuster to see the site before removing wet and moldy materials

dont.text: Do not disturb mold colonies without first sealing off the area — disturbing them can cause a huge release of spores into the air.

citations.quote: Disturbing mold colonies during cleanup can cause a huge release of spores into the air, so seal off the moldy areas from the rest of the house

dont.text: Do not ignore mold exposure risks — mold can trigger allergic reactions, asthma attacks, and may lower resistance to illness, especially in children, the elderly, and people in poor health.

citations.quote: Mold can trigger allergic reactions and asthma attacks, may lower resistance to illness, or have other effects

guidance.call_a_pro: For severe mold colonization (larger than 10 square feet), or if the building may contain asbestos or lead paint (common in historic buildings), hire a licensed mold remediation contractor with special training and equipment.

guidance.label: Roof
guidance.summary: After a flood, inspect the roof for water damage, damaged or missing materials, and compromised flashing. Document all damage with photographs before any work begins. Historic roofing materials should be repaired rather than replaced where possible, and a well-maintained roof will sustain less damage in future events.

do.text: Inspect the roof at least annually and after any flood or storm event — replace missing or damaged roofing shingles, slates, or tiles and repair flashing promptly.

citations.quote: inspect roofing at least once a year, preferably spring; replace missing or damaged roofing shingles, slates, or tiles; repair flashing; repair or replace cracked downspouts

do.text: Inspect and clean gutters regularly to keep drainage operational and prevent water from backing up into the roof structure.

citations.quote: Make weather-tight and operational; inspect and clean gutters as necessary depending on number of nearby trees, but at least twice a year

do.text: Document all damage with photographs before beginning any cleanup or repair — this is essential for insurance purposes and to record important historic building features.

citations.quote: Before you begin to clean up your historic property, it is important to carefully document any damage to the structure. This is essential not only for insurance purposes, but also to record important historic building features

do.text: Allow flood-saturated wood roof structures to dry naturally — a one-time flood event should not cause serious damage as long as the wood is allowed to dry afterward.

citations.quote: A one-off event such as a flood should not cause serious damage as long as the wood is allowed to dry afterwards

do.text: If the roof needs replacement, use the opportunity to incorporate storm-resistant materials, secure the roof decking, and strengthen the connections between the roof and the building structure.

citations.quote: The best time to upgrade a roof is when it needs replacement. Use this opportunity to incorporate new storm-resistant materials, secure the roof decking, and strengthen the connections

dont.text: Do not close up a wet roof assembly — trapped moisture in wood can lead to decay if the moisture content exceeds 28 percent, especially in wall cavities, sill plates, and behind impermeable finishes.

citations.quote: Problems occur when moisture is trapped in the wood and cannot escape. This can happen in wall cavities, in sill plates under floors, behind panelling and under impermeable finishes such as oil-based gloss paint

dont.text: Do not skip opening up the structure if needed to check for hidden moisture sources, assess the condition of the fabric, and allow trapped moisture to evaporate.

citations.quote: It may be necessary to open up the structure of the building to check for sources of moisture, to check on the condition of the fabric, and to allow trapped moisture to evaporate from masonry and timber

guidance.call_a_pro: If your roof has historic materials (slate, clay tile, wood shingle), contact your State Historic Preservation Office before replacing — compatible materials and techniques are required for historic properties.

guidance.label: Insurance, FEMA, and SBA
guidance.summary: Steps for flood insurance claims, FEMA Individual Assistance, and SBA disaster loans after a flood.

do.text: Check whether you have a separate flood insurance policy. Most homeowner policies don't cover flood damage unless flood coverage was bought separately.

citations.quote: most policies won't cover damage from floods or earthquakes unless you bought that coverage separately.

do.text: If you have insurance that covers the damage, file a claim. FEMA won't give home repair assistance for insured parts of the home if you don't file, and it needs your insurance settlement paperwork before it decides on help your insurance may cover.

citations.quote: An applicant with insurance for a covered peril will be ineligible for Home Repair Assistance for insured real property components when the applicant fails to file a claim
Insured applicants must provide documentation that identifies their insurance settlements or benefits before FEMA will consider their eligibility

do.text: Once it's safe to go inside, take photos or videos of the damaged areas and your belongings, and jot down notes about major damage. Keep all receipts for emergency repairs, and hotel receipts if you can't stay in your home.

citations.quote: Take photos or videos of the damaged areas and personal property. You also can jot down notes about any significant damage you see.
IMPORTANT: KEEP ALL RECEIPTS FOR EMERGENCY REPAIRS TO GIVE TO YOUR INSURANCE COMPANY.
If you can't stay in your home, save any hotel receipts. Your insurance company will need the receipts to repay you.

do.text: Gather photos or videos of the house and your belongings from before the flood, including ones on your phone or from family and friends, and any receipts showing when you bought damaged items.

citations.quote: Gather any photos or videos of your home and property before they were damaged or destroyed.
Review photos, for example on your cell phone or from family or friends, taken inside your home.
Include receipts from when you bought the damaged or destroyed items, if you have them.

do.text: Keep receipts, bills, and contractor estimates for disaster costs, since FEMA sometimes asks for them to verify losses. If you get FEMA money, keep records of how you spent it for at least three years.

citations.quote: In some cases, FEMA needs documentation from applicants such as receipts, bills, or estimates to verify losses.
Applicants should document how they used disaster funds and retain these records (e.g., receipts, invoices) for at least three years

do.text: If your home is in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area (a high-risk flood zone) and FEMA pays for home repair, home replacement, or personal property, you must buy and keep flood insurance (NFIP or private) for at least the amount of that aid. If you don't, you can't get FEMA help for flood damage in a future flood.

citations.quote: applicants who live in a designated SFHA and receive IHP assistance for Home Repair Assistance, Home Replacement Assistance, PHC, or Personal Property Assistance must obtain and maintain flood insurance coverage for at least the amount of disaster assistance they receive
Applicants may satisfy the insurance requirement by purchasing private insurance or a policy through the NFIP.
Applicants who do not obtain and maintain flood insurance will be ineligible for IHP assistance for flood-damaged real or personal property in future disasters with flood-related damage.

do.text: The flood insurance requirement stays with the house: it must be kept up at that address, and if you sell the house, it passes to the next owner. If you don't want the requirement, you have 30 days from FEMA's award letter to return the assistance for flood-insurable property.

citations.quote: Flood insurance coverage must be maintained at the address for as long as the address exists
If the home is sold or otherwise becomes owned by someone else, the requirement to purchase and maintain flood insurance carries over to any subsequent owner.
must return all disaster assistance they receive for NFIP-insurable real and personal property to FEMA no later than 30 days from the date of the award determination letter from FEMA.

dont.text: Don't make permanent repairs before talking with your insurance company. It may not pay for repairs it didn't authorize.

citations.quote: Don't make permanent repairs before talking with your insurance agent or insurance company. Your company may not pay for repairs it didn't authorize.

dont.text: Don't count on FEMA home repair money to restore historic materials. It is meant to make the home safe, sanitary, or functional, and it is priced at average quality.

citations.quote: Home Repair Assistance is intended to make the damaged home safe, sanitary, or functional.
Home Repair Assistance award amounts are based on repair or replacement of components that are of average quality, size, or capacity.

dont.text: Don't withdraw from the SBA process or decline an SBA loan if you still need help with personal property, vehicles, or group flood insurance. FEMA only helps with those after SBA, and it won't consider them again if you withdraw or decline.

citations.quote: Only applicants who do not qualify for a loan from the SBA may be eligible for assistance for the SBA-dependent category.
SBA-dependent ONA includes Personal Property Assistance, Transportation Assistance, and Group Flood Insurance Policy (GFIP).
Applicants who withdraw from the process or decline a loan from the SBA will not be referred back to FEMA for assistance with SBA-Dependent ONA.
